@geraldcombs  - Do you think this is a permissions issue with the buildbot?  Works fine "locally" for me, but there are certainly warnings in the libxml2 docs about loading external entries...

I'm not sure what's going on. If the pipeline job user was able to check out the repository it should be able to read the contents of _resources/protocols/diameter_. Note that this particular job uses the build directory name "🦈 build 🦈", but I'd expect that to be more of a problem on Windows.

Looks like: https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/libxml2/-/issues/287

Fixed, but only fairly recently:

https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/libxml2/-/commit/8ab1b122c47bfced2b59f52351507ebc1eb50218

Not sure if there was special handling for Windows, where directory names with spaces are more common.

The spaces and emojis were added for #17487 - it would be annoying to open that back up again thanks to libxml2, sigh.

So it sounds like our choices are:

1. Upgrade to newer version of libxml2 (that may not be supported on all platforms Wireshark supports)
2. Add more quotes somewhere in the CMakefile system? (I tried looking at !12256 but an obvious solution didn't jump out at me)

?

FWIW, I got the WiMax dictionary to pass the pipeline (!20111 ), but in its current state, it doesn't have additional files to "include" (that may be augmented by plugins outside of Wireshark source)
libxml2 isn't the only library that has this problem, BTW: #1827.

Excellent suggestion!  I hacked code to implement the solution (not very cross-platform friendly).

What exactly does that test prove? I can see what it does, but don't exactly like the idea of that happening during normal runtime. Should "more formal" code be in wsutil\\filesystem.c?  Should we try to apply a similar solution for libsmi?

[diameter_field_test_XML_PARSE_NO_XXE.txt](/uploads/1f333034075e081d7366920844727eb0/diameter_field_test_XML_PARSE_NO_XXE.txt)

[diameter_field_test_XML_PARSE_NOENT.txt](/uploads/c81b4aa28d007bc98d0b8e31db5ce915/diameter_field_test_XML_PARSE_NOENT.txt)

Here are the hf field differences when using XML_PARSE_NO_XXE on the diameter protocol, so I'd say it's "required" to not have the flag. libxml2 says it shouldn't be used on "untrusted data" and I'm not sure where Wireshark is in that. The files provided are "trusted", but the architecture allows for expandability with an updated diameter.XML or intentionally changing the already provided .XML "supporting" files. It's the XML specs more than parsing library that's to blame for the "security holes", so I don't think we should "roll our own XML parser" to try to address that. Ideally I'd like an option for "use local files only" and that would greatly limit the security holes to just run files provided in the diameter directory.

I could also be convinced to have a diameter protocol preference to control use of XML_PARSE_NO_XXE, but I would default it to "off" (don't use) to match backwards compatibility.  But even this seems dumb because if you don't use the diameter protocol, the fields aren't read through dictionary.XML and if you use the diameter protocol, I'd think you'd want all of the current diameter fields.

It's required to parse external entities because that's how all the vendor dictionaries are defined. (Theoretically they could be switched to XInclude, but that also has XXE attacks reported.)

It might be worth adding `XML_PARSE_NONET` to the options, not that the distributed files have network access, but we've never supported going out on the network to retrieve a dictionary or other external entity and libxml2 is removing support for that, so there's no real reason to add it now (and a theoretical attack vector.) (`XML_PARSE_NONET` only affects things if `XML_PARSE_NOENT` is enabled.)
Added XML_PARSE_NONET in latest patch

Running some quick profiling with `perf stat -d -r 500 ./run/tshark -nr ~/wireshark/test/captures/empty.pcap -Y diameter.version` (filtering for the Diameter field forces loading all the dictionaries), this is significantly slower than the existing parsing. The Diameter specific part is about twice as many instructions and takes twice as much time as the flex-based parser. (On my one box, it changes the time added for loading Diameter fields from some .02s to .04s.) That's of somewhat less importance because it only applies when using diameter fields, but I suppose building the DOM might be fairly heavyweight. I haven't looked into it more closely yet.

Use g_slist_prepend instead of g_slist_append?

skrev:
Converted to g_slist_append.  Hopefully that helps performance.
John, Could you please rerun the profiling?

That improved things considerably (from 0.02s slower to 0.01s slower on my one box), though it's still somewhat slower. (It's faster on a Wireshark DEBUG build, but that's kind of cheating; a Debug build results in the lex parser not being optimized, but libxml2 always is as it's the system library.)

Since it only occurs when actually registering the fields it's not as high priority to me since it doesn't occur on every startup.

Some of the slowness is in all the `g_slist_foreach` calls. Some is in the parsing itself. Note that the default xmlReadDocument creates a SAX2 parser with default handlers. To speed things up we'd probably need to do something similar with the XML dissector and override some of the SAX2 handlers and do our work in the SAX2 callbacks (and avoid creating some of the XML DOM structure.)

Would this be a "speed vs architectural layering" argument? Is it possible performance would improve with later versions of libxml2? (hoping you're using something recent, >= 2.13 with the refactoring).  I liked the simplicity of the xmlReadFile interface, especially for something that only executes once.

It's possible it would improve, but I doubt that it would ever be as fast simply because it creates the DOM structure, much of which we don't use and then free. I agree that the simplicity seems better, and I don't worry as much so long as the parsing is all happening later when Diameter is actually encountered or filtered for, as opposed to always on startup.
I just don't think there's a lot of room to improve without overriding the SAX2 handlers, but it may not be worth the complications here, unlike the XML dissector, which needed to parse on startup.
